title: Undoing Changes: Restore, Reset & Revert
description: Safely discard working tree edits, unstage files, adjust branch pointers with reset, and reverse public commits with revert.

blocks.content: Everyone makes mistakes. Git gives you several ways to undo things, but the right tool depends on whether the change has been committed yet and whether it has been shared with others.

## Undoing Uncommitted Changes

**Discard changes to a file** (goes back to how it was at the last commit):
```
git restore filename
```

**Remove a file from staging** (keeps your changes, just un-stages them):
```
git restore --staged filename
```

## Undoing Committed Changes

**Amend the very last commit** (only before pushing - fixes the message or adds a forgotten file):
```
git commit --amend -m "corrected message"
```

**Revert a commit** - this is the safe way to undo a commit that's already been shared. It creates a *new* commit that reverses the changes, so the history is preserved:
```
git revert abc1234
```

**Reset to an earlier commit** (dangerous on shared branches - rewrites history):
```
git reset --hard abc1234
```

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Need to undo something?"] --> B{"Already committed?"}
    B -- No --> C["git restore filename"]
    B -- Yes --> D{"Already pushed/shared?"}
    D -- No --> E["git commit --amend or git reset"]
    D -- Yes --> F["git revert - creates a new undo commit"]
```

blocks.question: A commit that introduced a bug has already been pushed and your teammates have pulled it. What is the safest way to undo it?
options: git reset --hard to remove it from history
Delete the files manually and commit again
git revert to create a new commit that undoes the changes
git restore to go back to an earlier state
blocks.explanation: `git revert` creates a new commit that reverses the changes from a specific commit. History is preserved and your teammates' copies stay compatible. `git reset --hard` rewrites history, which causes problems for anyone who already has the commit.

blocks.prompt: Discard the unstaged changes in a file called app.py (bring it back to the last committed state).
